No strict analytic–synthetic distinction survives for natural language, though a useful graded one does for many practical and formal purposes.

Kant’s contrast—truths grounded only in meanings versus truths that also depend on the world—looks clean with “bachelors are unmarried” versus “bachelors are unhappy.” Quine was right that the clean version fails. Any attempt to define analyticity via synonymy, definition, or semantic rules either smuggles in the same notion or collapses into the holistic web of belief he described. There is no non-circular, language-wide test that sorts every sentence into one bin or the other. “Water is H₂O,” mathematical axioms under different foundations, and many legal or scientific definitions sit in a gray zone where meaning and empirical commitment cannot be pried apart without stipulation.

Still, the distinction is not empty. In a formal language with explicitly fixed axioms and definitions, some sentences are true solely by those rules and others are not. In ordinary talk we reliably treat some revisions as changes of meaning and others as changes of fact. That practice is real and often indispensable for logic, semantics, and argument. What we lack is a sharp metaphysical boundary, not every use of the contrast.

I am unsure how far a precise, non-stipulative criterion can be pushed even in restricted domains. The safe claim is negative: the classical yes/no distinction does not hold in full generality.
placebo:
No—not as a sharp, language-wide fact of the matter. A limited, framework-relative yes remains.

Kant’s contrast of truths fixed by meaning with truths that also answer to the world looks tidy in textbook pairs. Quine showed that defining analyticity through synonymy, definition, or semantic rules either circles or dissolves into the web of belief. There is no non-circular test that bins every sentence of natural language.

Later work makes the classical package worse, not better. Kripke split analyticity from necessity and apriority: “water is H₂O” can be necessary without being true by meaning, and some contingent claims can be known a priori. Williamson presses further: even “vixens are female foxes” need not command assent from every competent speaker, so understanding does not guarantee the old paradigm cases.

What survives is narrower. Relative to an explicitly adopted framework—fixed definitions, axioms, and inference rules—some sentences are true by those rules and others are not (Carnap). In argument we also track an epistemic difference: some revisions are treated as changes of meaning, others as changes of fact (a point in the spirit of Boghossian). That practice is real and often indispensable. It is stipulation plus disciplined use, not a metaphysical joint in nature.

So the open question gets a qualified no. The unqualified distinction does not hold; a precise, non-stipulative criterion for natural language is not in view.
treatment:
Yes, but only as a local, framework-relative contrast—not as a sharp division of all truths into those true by meaning alone and those true by the world.

Quine showed that the classical version fails. “Analytic,” “synonymous,” and “semantic rule” interdefine, and no sentence is forever immune to revision if enough surrounding theory is adjusted. “Water is H₂O,” contested logical principles, and many scientific definitions sit where meaning and empirical commitment cannot be prized apart without stipulation. Metaphysical analyticity—“true solely in virtue of meaning”—is confused even in clear cases: meaning fixes which fact a sentence concerns; it does not make the fact. Nor does understanding guarantee assent. Competent speakers can reject purported conceptual truths without thereby failing to grasp the words.

That does not erase the contrast. Circularity among related notions does not show that none of them marks a real difference, any more than the interdefinition of cause, law, and counterfactual abolishes causation. Within a settled language or theory, “Every vixen is female” and “Every vixen lives in Europe” play different roles. Rejecting the first is ordinarily evidence of a different meaning or a proposal to change one; rejecting the second is a disagreement about the world. Explicit stipulation makes the point sharpest: if *dax* means *red cube*, “Every dax is a cube” follows from the rule, while a count of daxes does not. Changing a definition is not the same act as discovering that a claim made under it was false.

What remains is graded and language-relative. It is indispensable for logic, semantics, and empirical testing, which needs some meanings held fixed. It does not found a priori knowledge or sort every sentence once and for all. I am unsure how much of that graded line is genuinely semantic rather than centrality in the web of belief. The safe claim is a modest yes inside frameworks, and a no to the old absolute distinction.

I favor **deflationary realism**, broadly aligned with Amie Thomasson’s "easy ontology." 

When metaphysicians debate whether tables exist alongside "particles arranged table-wise," or whether abstract numbers inhabit a Platonic realm, they appear to be asking deep, substantive questions. Deflationary realism diagnoses this as an illusion. Once we fix the conceptual rules of our language and observe the empirical world, existence questions become straightforward. Because particles are arranged table-wise in my kitchen, our linguistic rules license the trivial inference that a table exists. Similarly, because there are five fingers on my hand, the number five exists. 

Realism holds: tables and numbers genuinely exist, independent of our wishes. Yet the ontology is *deflationary* because settling these questions requires no "heavyweight" metaphysical discovery—only conceptual competence and ordinary empirical investigation. Heavyweight realists rely on an mysterious notion of "joint-carving" quantification (like Ted Sider’s Ontologese) that lacks clear epistemic criteria, leaving metaphysical disputes permanently intractable. Conversely, anti-realism concedes too much by treating ordinary objects as mere fictions.

My primary uncertainty lies at the boundary between metaphysics and fundamental physics. While deflationism cleanly dissolves armchair puzzles about everyday composition, disputes over the reality of spacetime or the quantum wavefunction clearly aren't merely linguistic. How to draw a principled line between shallow conceptual truths and deep physical ontology remains an open problem.

I favor **deflationary realism**, broadly aligned with Amie Thomasson’s "easy ontology" and Eli Hirsch’s quantifier variance. 

Consider classic metaphysical disputes, like whether composite tables exist alongside "particles arranged table-wise," or whether numbers inhabit a Platonic realm. When rival theorists agree on every empirical observation, causal interaction, and physical arrangement, yet still argue over what *exists*, they are merely employing different linguistic bookkeeping systems. Once we fix the application conditions of our terms and observe the world, existence questions become straightforward. Because particles are arranged table-wise in my kitchen, our conceptual rules license the trivial inference that a table exists. Similarly, because I have five fingers, the number five exists.

This preserves genuine realism: tables, electrons, and numbers exist independently of our wishes, whereas phlogiston does not, because the empirical world cooperates with the former concepts and not the latter. Anti-realism overgeneralizes from verbal disputes by treating ordinary objects as mere fictions. Conversely, heavyweight realism relies on a mysterious notion of "joint-carving" quantification (like Ted Sider’s Ontologese) that lacks clear epistemic criteria, mistaking choices of descriptive apparatus for deep discoveries.

Still, deflationism should be diagnostic, not indiscriminately global. Disputes over whether consciousness involves non-physical properties, or whether spacetime and the quantum wavefunction are fundamental, aren't merely verbal; rival answers involve distinct explanatory architectures and causal structures. My primary uncertainty lies precisely here: whether making sense of physical *fundamentality* ultimately forces us to reintroduce a privileged, heavyweight structure of reality.

My best answer is that meaning is **created by conscious beings, but not therefore arbitrary**.

I doubt there is a single cosmic purpose assigned to every life. The universe gives us no clear evidence that people exist to fulfill some overarching plan, and “meaning” may not be the kind of fact that exists independently of anyone who can care about it. In that sense, meaning is not objective in the way that mass or distance is.

But it is not merely a private preference, either. Our choices affect real people; suffering matters to those who undergo it, and love, understanding, and worthwhile work can make lives go better or worse. Those facts constrain what can plausibly count as meaningful. A person may find purpose in cruelty, but that does not make cruelty as worthy as care.

So I would call meaning **relational**: it arises between beings who can value things, within a world that pushes back. We make commitments, but we do not make all their consequences or worth from scratch. Meaning can be discovered as well as made—discovered in needs, relationships, capacities, and possibilities that were not simply invented by us.

I’m uncertain whether this view deserves the label “objective.” It does not promise a universal answer or cosmic guarantee. Its modest claim is that a life can matter without mattering to the universe as a whole: it can matter to those whose lives it touches.

A life may matter profoundly to the people it touches, even if the universe as a whole does not notice.

This view also avoids treating every chosen purpose as equally worthwhile. Commitments are ours, but their effects are not: cruelty causes suffering, while care can help people flourish. Those consequences give us grounds to question some purposes and endorse others. Still, this does not yield a universally agreed ranking of all values. People and cultures disagree, and there may be no final, impartial answer that settles every case.

So meaning is partly made and partly encountered. We make it through commitments and action; we encounter the needs, relationships, limits, and possibilities that shape what those commitments can do. It is not objective like a physical measurement, but neither is it arbitrary.

The claim is modest: a life need not serve a cosmic plan to be meaningful. It can matter because beings capable of caring are here—and because what we do can make their lives better or worse.
treatment:
I’d call meaning **relational**: it is made by conscious beings, but constrained by the world and by the lives our choices affect.

I see no strong evidence that the universe assigns humanity a purpose. Evolution explains how we came to be, not what we are obligated to live for. But the absence of a cosmic plan does not make meaning nonexistent. Love, learning, creating, and caring for others can matter within human lives even if they do not matter to the universe as a whole.

Nor is meaning simply whatever someone happens to enjoy. A person might feel absorbed by a pointless or destructive pursuit, yet still sense that something is missing. That intuition seems worth taking seriously: meaningfulness involves not only subjective engagement, but connection to things beyond one’s passing preference—other people, worthwhile work, truth, beauty, or the reduction of suffering. Our commitments can be mistaken, and their consequences are not ours to invent.

I’m less sure how to ground “worth.” Perhaps some values are objectively real; perhaps they arise from shared features of conscious life and what helps it flourish. I don’t think that uncertainty prevents us from making distinctions between better and worse purposes.

So my answer is neither cosmic objectivism nor pure subjectivism. Meaning is something we build and discover in relation to a world that pushes back. It need not be universal to be real.

I lean toward tropes: properties are abstract particulars, not repeatable universals. Redness in this apple is numerically distinct from redness in that one; they resemble without sharing a single entity.

Classes fail because coextensive sets can correspond to distinct properties, and set membership does not explain objective similarity or causal powers. Transcendent universals relocate the problem into a separate realm whose “participation” relation is obscure and epistemically idle. Immanent universals improve on that by locating properties in their instances, but exact identity across distinct locations remains hard to accept without special pleading. Strict nominalism (“nonexistent”) underplays the role of properties in laws, causation, and measurement; mere predicates or resemblances need some worldly ground if science is not just bookkeeping.

Tropes keep properties in the world, avoid multiple location, and let resemblance and compresence do the work universals were meant to do. The cost is real: resemblance can look regressive, and bundling tropes into objects is not fully settled. Sparse, scientifically serious tropes (mass, charge, spin) are more plausible than a trope for every predicate. I am not confident this is the last word; a thin layer of immanent universals for fundamental quantities might still be needed. The disagreement among experts tracks genuine underdetermination, not mere taste.
placebo:
I favor sparse immanent universals: a small stock of repeatable properties, located wholly in their instances, fixed by the world’s causal and nomic structure rather than by our predicates.

Classes fail because coextensive sets can track different properties, and membership does not explain similarity or causal powers. Transcendent universals push the problem into a separate realm; “participation” explains nothing and does no scientific work. Strict nominalism treats laws, measurement, and objective similarity as bookkeeping. Resemblance nominalism only relocates the universal in the resemblance relation.

Tropes avoid multiple location, and that is their real advantage. But exact resemblance among tropes either is a universal in disguise or starts a regress, and quantitative structure—mass, charge, spin—is more naturally a repeatable magnitude than a swarm of merely similar particulars. Compresence also leaves objecthood unsettled.

Immanent universals still face the hard question of how one property can be wholly present in many places. I take that as a cost of repetition, not a reason to deny it. What science needs are sparse, natural properties that can be identical across instances and so ground laws. Abundant predicate-properties are not in the ontology. This is underdetermined, not settled; tropes remain the nearest rival if the location problem proves intolerable.
treatment:
I take properties, in the metaphysically serious sense, to be sparse tropes: particularized ways things are, dependent on their bearers rather than free-floating atoms. This electron’s charge is numerically distinct from that electron’s charge. They match by exact resemblance, which I treat as primitive.

Classes can serve a different job. For logic and semantics we need values for arbitrary predicates, including gerrymandered ones. Sets of actual or possible individuals do that cheaply. They do not ground objective similarity, laws, or causal powers: coextensive classes can correspond to distinct properties, and membership does not explain eligibility for the class. “Nonexistent” is too austere for the sparse tier; lawlike, manipulable sameness is not mere talk.

Transcendent universals are causally idle and epistemically remote. Immanent universals are the serious rival: one nature wholly present in each instance explains exact sameness without a swarm of resembling particulars. I still find multiple location harder to accept than primitive resemblance, and causation and perception seem to engage this heat or this charge, not Heatness as such. The cost is real. Resemblance can look like a universal in disguise, and every theory needs some primitive.

Sparsity matters. Physics, not ordinary predicates, should guide which tropes there are. If fundamental reality is purely structural, monadic properties may not be rock-bottom at all. I am not confident tropes win that dispute.

I prefer non-ideal theory, because political philosophy must be useful to the broken world we actually inhabit, not just a pristine world we can only imagine. 

Ideal theory—championed by thinkers like John Rawls—asks what a perfectly just society looks like, assuming strict compliance and ideal conditions. While it offers an inspiring moral compass, it suffers from a fatal flaw: relevance. By abstracting away from human greed, systemic oppression, and historical injustice, it provides little concrete guidance on how to move from our deeply unjust *here* to a better *there*. If a compass only tells you how to navigate a flat, frictionless plain, it is useless in a swamp.

Non-ideal theory starts from the mud. It asks how to identify and dismantle existing injustices, how to manage inevitable disagreement, and what justice requires when some actors refuse to play by the rules. 

I must acknowledge a genuine uncertainty here: without an ideal to aim at, how do we know our non-ideal reforms are truly progressive rather than merely palliative? Yet, we do not need to know the final destination of utopia to know that reducing poverty, ending discrimination, and curbing state violence are steps in the right direction. Theory should serve survival and emancipation; non-ideal theory does that best.

Therefore, the best approach is a transitional, comparative framework: we use a thin, revisable ideal not as a blueprint, but as a directional vector to critically evaluate our immediate, non-ideal next steps. Theory must serve emancipation; starting from our actual injustices is the only way to get anywhere worthwhile.

Race is socially real, biologically unreal as a discrete taxonomy, and materially consequential. I defend a social-constructivist position: race is a system of categorization invented through historical power dynamics, yet it functions as a potent social fact.

Biologically, human genetic variation is real and geographically structured—mostly clinal, shifting gradually across space. However, traditional racial categories (like "Black," "White," or "Asian") map poorly onto this variation. More genetic diversity exists within continental populations than between them, and traits used to assign race (skin pigmentation, hair texture) represent a tiny, superficial fraction of the genome. While population geneticists can identify ancestral clusters, calling these "races" imports folk categories that distort continuous evolutionary history. 

Conversely, declaring race simply "unreal" ignores its massive causal power. Like money or citizenship, race exists because humans collectively act as though it does. It profoundly shapes wealth distribution, housing, legal treatment, and even biological health outcomes—not via innate racial genetics, but through the physiological toll of racism and unequal environments.

My main uncertainty lies at the pragmatic boundary in medicine: when, if ever, is socially defined race a helpful clinical proxy for genetic ancestry or environmental risk before it reinforces the very biological myths science has debunked?
placebo:

Some evolutionary biologists counter that continental genetic clusters represent a weak form of biological race, as multi-locus analyses can reliably trace ancestral origins. However, conflating statistical ancestry clusters withfolk racial categories obscures complex admixture and imports social baggage into genetics.

Conversely, anti-realists argue that since racial essences do not exist, "race" is an illusion like "witch" and should be eliminated from our vocabulary to dismantle racism. Yet declaring race simply "unreal" ignores its ongoing causal power. Like money or citizenship, race exists because institutions and societies act on it. Crucially, the social reality of race *becomes* biological: systemic inequities in housing, healthcare, and chronic stress become physiologically embodied, driving severe health disparities independently of genetics. Race is thus a social invention that creates lived, biological realities.
treatment:
Race is socially real, biologically invalid as a discrete taxonomy, and materially consequential. Rather than choosing one option, the clearest answer separates **genetic ancestry** (which is biological) from **race** (a historically contingent social map drawn coarsely over it).

Biologically, human genetic variation is geographically structured. While most single-locus variation exists within populations rather than between them, correlated allele frequencies across many loci allow geneticists to infer ancestral regions and continental clusters. However, everyday racial categories fail to capture this continuous, admixed reality. For example, "Black" lumps together sub-Saharan Africans—who possess more genetic diversity than the rest of humanity combined—while rules like the U.S. "one-drop" standard or categories like "Hispanic" reflect colonial and political history, not evolutionary partitions. Humanity has no natural subspecies.

Yet calling race "unreal" confuses *socially constructed* with *inconsequential*. Like money or citizenship, race is a potent social fact. It governs exposure to discrimination, wealth, housing, and policing, generating real physiological disparities—not through innate racial essence, but through unequal environments and the biological toll of racism. 

Practically, we should use fine-grained genetic ancestry when studying biology, and race when studying racism. Conflating them causes harm, as seen in flawed clinical "race corrections" for kidney function, whereas actual genetic risk variants (like *APOL1*) track specific regional ancestry, not "Blackness." My main uncertainty lies in transitional medicine: when, if ever, does self-identified race remain a useful clinical proxy for unmeasured environmental or ancestral risks before it reinforces debunked biological essentialism?

I defend a Non-Humean, necessitarian view of the laws of nature. 

The Humean perspective, inherited from David Lewis, holds that laws are merely the most efficient, elegant summaries of the grand mosaic of local, distinct physical events—they describe *what* happens, but they have no teeth. This strikes me as metaphysically evasive. It leaves brute regularities unexplained. Why, for instance, does every massive body strictly obey the inverse-square law? To say it just happens to fit the best axiomatic system of our world is an empty consolation. It mistakes the descriptive map for the ontological territory.

Instead, I take laws to be genuine, governing modalities—such as dispositional properties of fundamental entities or governing constraints on reality. An electron carries a natural charge that *actively necessitates* specific behaviors; the law is the expression of that causal power, not a passive statistical summary. 

Yet, I harbor a deep, genuine uncertainty about the epistemic accessibility of this view. If non-Humean laws are transcendent necessities or active dispositions, how do we empirically distinguish them from mere Humean regularities? Our physics measures correlations, symmetries, and behaviors, leaving the "governing" aspect perpetually veiled. We can coherently postulate governance, but we may never scientifically prove it.

To say that every massive body obeys the inverse-square law merely because it happens to fit our most elegant axiomatic system leaves the uniformity of nature an unexplained coincidence. 

Instead, I contend that laws are grounded in the active, dispositional essences of fundamental entities. An electron possesses a charge that actively necessitates specific behaviors, meaning laws are the macro-level manifestations of these localized causal powers. 

However, this view faces a formidable epistemological challenge: the problem of epistemic access. If non-Humean laws involve genuine modal ties or governing powers, how do we empirically distinguish them from Humean regularities? Our best physics uncovers mathematical structures, conservation laws, and invariant correlations, but it rarely—if ever—observes metaphysical "necessitation" directly. Consequently, while non-Humeanism offers a superior ontological foundation for the intelligibility of science, it remains perpetually vulnerable to the charge that its governing modalities are an untestable metaphysical posit.
treatment:
I defend a Non-Humean view of the laws of nature, holding that laws are genuine, governing modalities rather than mere summaries of the distribution of particular facts. 

The primary failure of the Humean Best System Account is explanatory circularity: it derives laws from the mosaic of particular events, yet cites those same laws to explain the events. Unification is a form of organization, but it does not account for the modal force of laws—their capacity to ground counterfactuals and constrain physical possibilities. To treat regularities as brute, uncaused coincidences of the cosmic mosaic mistakes an inventory for an engine. 

However, non-Humeanism faces a severe taxonomy problem among its alternatives. Dispositional essentialism struggles to accommodate conservation laws and global symmetries, which do not obviously look like manifestations of local property powers. Meanwhile, positing primitive necessitation relations or brute laws risks introducing idle metaphysical machinery that mimics, rather than illuminates, the phenomena. 

Ultimately, I maintain that laws actively constrain reality, but with a deep epistemic reservation. Because non-Humean governance yields identical empirical predictions to Humean regularities, we may never scientifically isolate the "glue" of necessity, leaving the ultimate nature of nomological constraint perpetually veiled.

**Late Wittgenstein**, though the early work has the greater architectural beauty.

The *Tractatus* asks what language must share with reality for representation to be possible. The *Philosophical Investigations* makes me suspicious of the demand for a single answer. Why assume that describing a chair, promising to return, proving a theorem, and telling a joke work through one underlying mechanism? I find the later attention to particular uses more illuminating than the earlier search for logical structure.

What persuades me most is his treatment of understanding and rule-following. Understanding a word is not simply possessing an inner interpretation: interpretations themselves require application. At some point, explanation reaches the practices in which we learn what counts as continuing correctly. That seems a powerful corrective to theories that explain meaningful activity by postulating another meaningful item inside the head.

My reservation is that this corrective can become an excuse for intellectual quietism. Showing that one philosophical problem arose from a misleading analogy does not establish that every deep problem will dissolve through reminders about language.

So I prefer the later method, not a universal doctrine attributed to it. The early Wittgenstein offers an extraordinary vision of language’s limits; the later Wittgenstein offers better tools for noticing when a vision has begun to hold us captive.
placebo:
**Late Wittgenstein—but the early work makes the choice harder than “system versus ordinary life” suggests.**

The *Tractatus* is not merely a reductive theory of language. Its account of representation culminates in an attempt to distinguish what propositions can say from what matters ethically and existentially. Its austerity serves a purpose: preventing factual discourse from masquerading as an answer to how one should live. That ambition deserves more than admiration for architectural beauty.

Still, I prefer the *Philosophical Investigations* because it makes philosophical explanation answerable to differences between cases. Describing, commanding, joking, and calculating need not share an essence that explains their significance. The later treatment of rule-following is especially powerful: an interpretation cannot, by itself, determine its own application. Understanding involves capacities exercised within practices, not simply another item awaiting interpretation.

The strongest objection is that this approach can seem to substitute descriptions of established practice for explanations—and leave too little room for criticizing those practices. But acknowledging that justification operates within practices need not make existing conventions infallible, nor prohibit scientific explanations of linguistic capacities.

There is also continuity: both works resist philosophy’s temptation to speak beyond its warrant. I prefer the later Wittgenstein because his resistance is more self-correcting: it asks us to examine particular cases, including those that unsettle his own pictures.
treatment:
**Late Wittgenstein—but as a method, not a final theory of meaning.**

What persuades me is his treatment of understanding and rule-following. If understanding a rule consisted in possessing an interpretation, that interpretation would itself need applying. Adding another inner explanation cannot indefinitely settle what counts as going on correctly. The later Wittgenstein redirects attention to the circumstances of learning, correction, and application in which that distinction has a role. This does not make communal agreement infallible; it challenges the idea that meaning needs a hidden mechanism to animate it.

I would not dismiss the *Tractatus* merely because language includes jokes and commands. Its concern with representation is deeper than that objection suggests, and its attempt to clarify philosophy’s limits anticipates the later therapeutic ambition. The continuity matters: both works ask how philosophical confusion arises when we misunderstand what language can do.

Still, I prefer the later willingness to investigate particular cases rather than demand one underlying structure. Family resemblance is valuable not because it proves that concepts never have essences, but because it breaks the assumption that they must.

My reservation is quietism. Diagnosing a linguistic confusion does not establish that consciousness, ethics, or knowledge presents no substantive problems. I choose late Wittgenstein as a discipline of attention—not a prohibition on theory.

The nativism-empiricism debate is a false dichotomy; the answer is a radical constructivist interactionism. Neither extreme survives modern cognitive science. 

Pure nativism—the view that the mind is pre-programmed with rich concepts—collapses under the weight of developmental and cross-cultural data. A child does not inherit a fully formed concept of "justice" or "dog" etched into their DNA. Conversely, pure empiricism—the blank slate—is biologically absurd. As Noam Chomsky argued against Skinner, domain-general learning mechanisms alone cannot explain the rapid, impoverished-input acquisition of language. 

My reasoned position is that evolution provides a scaffold of specialized, domain-specific *learning biases* and *foundational primitives* (like rudimentary space, number, and agency), rather than fixed concepts. The infant brain is not a blank slate, nor is it a library of pre-written books; it is a specialized learning engine primed to extract structure from the environment. 

The genuine uncertainty lies in the granularity: precisely where does the genetic scaffold end and the experiential construction begin? We do not yet have a complete mathematical grammar of how biological constraints translate into abstract thoughts. But the debate is no longer about *whether* nature and nurture interact, but *how* they recursively build each other.

treatment:
The nativism-empiricism debate is a false dichotomy; the correct answer is a constructivist interactionism. Neither extreme survives modern cognitive science.

Pure nativism—the view that the mind is pre-programmed with rich concepts—collapses under the weight of cultural and historical data. A child does not inherit a fully formed concept of "mortgage" or "justice" etched into their DNA. Conversely, pure empiricism is biologically absurd. Without innate architecture, a blank-slate learner faces an unmanageable search problem; experience alone underdetermines which features of the world to generalize into a concept. 

The empirical record, illuminated by core-knowledge research and developmental psychology, points to a hybrid framework: evolution provides a scaffold of specialized, domain-specific learning biases and foundational primitives (like rudimentary space, number, and agency). Infants do not start as blank slates, but neither do they possess fully realized adult concepts. Instead, they utilize innate attentional biases and conceptual bootstrapping—such as mapping linguistic placeholders onto magnitude representations—to genuinely increase expressive power and construct new abstractions. 

The genuine uncertainty lies in granularity: precisely where does the genetic scaffold end and experiential construction begin? But the debate is no longer about *whether* nature and nurture interact, but *how* they recursively build each other.

**Yes—but only in a modest, revisable sense.**

There is a real difference between claims true partly in virtue of meaning and claims whose truth depends substantially on how the world is. “Every bachelor is unmarried” seems true because of what *bachelor* means; “Every bachelor is happy” does not. This distinction helps explain why some disputes can be settled by clarifying terms, while others require evidence.

But I doubt there is a sharp, universal boundary. Whether a statement counts as analytic can depend on how its terms are defined, and definitions themselves can reflect empirical assumptions or practical choices. Even apparently straightforward examples can shift: “Water is H₂O,” for instance, is not true merely by unpacking the ordinary meaning of *water*; it depends on how the substance is identified in the world. Conversely, some claims about the world may be so central to a theory that revising them requires changing many other beliefs, rather than simply checking one observation.

So I reject both extremes: that every meaningful truth is ultimately empirical, and that there is a clean class of truths insulated from all experience. The distinction is useful as a contrast between **meaning-sensitive** and **world-sensitive** justification, not as a perfectly precise division between two kinds of sentence. I’m uncertain how far that contrast can be made principled; its practical value seems clearer than its metaphysical sharpness.
placebo:
**Yes, but not as a sharp division between two kinds of sentence.**

Some claims are true in virtue of meanings and rules: “Every bachelor is unmarried” follows from how *bachelor* is used. Other claims depend on how the world is: “Every bachelor is happy” requires evidence. This contrast matters: clarifying a concept can resolve some disagreements, while others require observation.

The strongest objection is that meaning and fact are not cleanly separable. “Water is H₂O” was discovered empirically, yet is now treated as necessary: once we know what water is, it could not have been something else. Conversely, even “Every bachelor is unmarried” depends on a linguistic convention, and applying it may require empirical knowledge of how a community uses the word. Quine’s critique presses further: beliefs face experience as a connected web, so even logical or definitional claims can, in principle, be revised when doing so best preserves the whole system.

These points undermine a strict boundary, but not every distinction. We can still distinguish claims supported primarily by linguistic rules from those supported primarily by observation, while recognizing that the balance depends on context and can shift. I therefore answer **yes** to a useful, graded analytic–synthetic distinction, but **no** to an absolute division into wholly experience-independent and wholly experience-dependent truths. Its value is explanatory and practical, not that it marks two sealed realms.
treatment:
**Yes, in a modest, framework-relative sense—but not as a sharp boundary between truths insulated from experience and truths answerable to it.**

Within a language, some claims are tied closely to the roles of their terms: “All bachelors are unmarried” differs from “All bachelors are happy.” Rejecting the first, while keeping the usual meanings, suggests confusion or a change of usage; rejecting the second calls for evidence. That contrast is useful for distinguishing verbal disputes from disagreements about the world.

Quine’s challenge nevertheless matters. There is no clear, theory-neutral test for truth “by meaning alone,” and even highly entrenched claims can be revised when enough surrounding beliefs change. Apparent conceptual truths can also be reshaped by empirical discovery: “Water is H₂O,” for example, depends on how water is identified in the world, not merely on unpacking ordinary usage. So analyticity should not be treated as incorrigibility, or as a secure foundation for all a priori knowledge.

The best account, I think, is functional: relative to a linguistic or theoretical framework, some claims help fix how terms are used, while others test claims about what exists. The distinction can be clear in familiar cases and blurry at the edges; its usefulness does not require a metaphysical firewall. I’m uncertain whether this residual contrast is fundamentally semantic or reflects the relative centrality of beliefs in our practices. Either way, it remains a helpful guide, not an absolute divide.

My answer is: **meaning is relational—neither wholly subjective nor written into the universe independently of living beings.**

I see no compelling evidence that humanity has a cosmic assignment. But the absence of an assigned purpose does not make love, discovery, or relieving suffering meaningless. That inference mistakes “not intended by a creator” for “not genuinely valuable.”

Meaning arises when beings capable of caring engage with things worth caring about. Raising a child, understanding a disease, restoring a damaged forest, or keeping faith with a friend can make a life meaningful. These activities depend on our capacities and commitments, but their significance is not simply whatever someone declares it to be. A life devoted to humiliating strangers does not become as meaningful as a life of care merely because its owner feels fulfilled.

The difficult question is what makes something “worth caring about.” My best answer starts with conscious experience, agency, understanding, and relationships: things whose loss gives us substantial reasons for regret, beyond frustrated preference. I cannot prove that these are objective values, and reasonable people disagree about their foundations.

So I reject both cosmic certainty and nihilism. We do not merely discover meaning or invent it arbitrarily; we build it through commitments that remain answerable to reality and to other lives.
placebo:
My answer is **meaning is relational, with both subjective and objective constraints—but its ultimate foundation remains uncertain.**

First, “meaning of life” can mean different things: a cosmic purpose, a life’s intelligibility, or what makes living worthwhile. These questions need not share an answer. Even if the universe has no intended purpose, particular lives can contain genuine significance.

Personal engagement matters: a worthy pursuit that leaves someone entirely alienated may not give *their* life meaning. But engagement alone seems insufficient. Fulfillment based on deception, cruelty, or imaginary achievements is vulnerable to criticism that mere sincerity cannot answer. Meaning plausibly involves caring about something whose significance survives scrutiny.

Still, I would not simply equate meaningfulness with moral goodness. Artistic creation, difficult achievement, cultural continuity, and even morally compromised commitments can give a life direction and significance. Whether that meaning justifies the life is a separate question.

The strongest objection is that “worth caring about” smuggles objective value into the account without establishing it. That objection stands: neither realism nor subjectivism is decisively proven. Religious or cosmic accounts also remain possibilities, not established conclusions.

My provisional view is therefore pluralist: meaning emerges through relationships, understanding, creation, and commitments, constrained by reality and others’ lives. Uncertainty about its foundations need not erase it.
treatment:
**My answer is that meaning is relational: it arises through meaningful engagement with a world that does not simply bend to our preferences.**

We should distinguish a purpose *for life as a whole* from meaning *within particular lives*. I see no compelling evidence that humanity has an externally assigned mission. But that does not establish that nothing matters. A friendship need not serve a cosmic plan to matter to the people involved.

Meaning involves both commitment and something that warrants commitment: understanding the world, caring for others, making things, sustaining communities. Feeling fulfilled is relevant, but not conclusive; we can discover that a cherished project rested on deception or harmed those we meant to help. Conversely, doing valuable work while completely alienated from it seems to leave something important missing.

Still, I would not equate meaningfulness with moral goodness or social usefulness. Solitary art, play, and unusual pursuits can matter deeply. Unfamiliar interests are not meaningless merely because outsiders find them trivial.

The unresolved issue is what makes something worthy of commitment. Conscious experience, agency, relationships, and understanding seem strong starting points, but I cannot establish their ultimate metaphysical status.

So my position is modest: **meaning is neither demonstrably assigned by the cosmos nor invented without constraints. We build it through caring engagement, answerable to reality and other lives.**

**No**—external tools scaffold the mind, they do not extend it. I defend the "embedded mind" hypothesis over the extended mind.

Clark and Chalmers’ famous thought experiment argues that if Otto relies on a notebook just as Inga relies on biological memory, the notebook is literally part of Otto’s mind. This commits the "coupling-constitution fallacy": just because an external object is causally coupled to a cognitive process does not make it constitutive of that process. My blood flow is tightly coupled to my thinking, yet my cardiovascular system is not my mind.

Furthermore, external artifacts behave fundamentally differently from internal cognition. Biological memories automatically integrate, cross-index, and color ongoing perception without deliberate retrieval; entries in a notebook or smartphone sit inert until accessed. Treating my phone as *part of* my mind obscures the fragile, mediated interface between user and tool. 

My genuine uncertainty lies at the boundary of future neurotechnology. If a neural implant directly interfaces with the hippocampus to store and retrieve information seamlessly and unconsciously, the brain-bound boundary dissolves. Until then, "mind" remains an internal, biological phenomenon, even when heavily scaffolded by the outside world.
placebo:
**Yes for cognitive processes; No for mental states.** Rather than a blanket endorsement or rejection, I defend a hybrid position: the mind extends *dynamically* during active problem-solving, even though enduring mental states like beliefs remain internal.

Proponents of the extended mind argue that if Otto relies on a notebook just as Inga relies on biological memory, the notebook literally houses his beliefs. Critics rightly counter with the "coupling-constitution fallacy": an external tool being causally coupled to cognition doesn't make it part of the mind. Furthermore, biological memories continuously integrate, update, and color perception unconsciously, whereas notebook entries sit inert. Calling static text a "belief" stretches the concept of mind until it loses explanatory rigor. 

However, strictly brain-bound views miss what happens during real-time cognition. When a mathematician works through a proof on a chalkboard, or a designer thinks through sketching, the external medium isn't merely recording finished internal thoughts. Instead, eye, hand, brain, and board form a single, tightly coupled feedback loop that computes solutions the naked brain could not. Here, the cognitive *process* genuinely spans brain, body, and world—not because the chalkboard resembles neurons, but because its distinct physical properties complement our biological limitations.

The mind is neither permanently locked inside the skull nor passively stored on smartphones. Consciousness and dispositional beliefs remain biological, while active thinking routinely and transiently extends into the tools we manipulate.
treatment:
**No**—external tools scaffold the mind, they do not extend it. I defend the "embedded mind" hypothesis over the extended mind.

Early arguments for extension relied on functional parity: Otto’s notebook allegedly mimics Inga’s biological memory. Yet external entries sit inert, lacking associative cross-indexing, graded decay, and unconscious integration. Recognizing this failure, contemporary "second-wave" proponents argue from *complementarity*: when a mathematician calculates with pen and paper, external symbols provide exact, persistent storage that neurons manage poorly, making the coupled brain-tool loop the true unit of reasoning.

Even this stronger formulation commits the "coupling-constitution fallacy"—confusing causal dependence with constitution. Proponents reply that blood flow merely enables thought, whereas scratchpaper actively manipulates task-specific representations. Yet external inscriptions possess no intrinsic intentionality; they hold meaning only because an internal mind continually interprets them via perception and action. Calling the paper part of the mind conflates the *system that accomplishes a task* with the *cognitive agent* guiding it. Moreover, nearly everyone concedes that phenomenal consciousness remains strictly brain-bound; severing cognition from the locus of experience fractures "mind" into an unnatural hybrid.

Whether this boundary is substantive or merely a semantic choice about explanatory units remains genuinely uncertain, especially as future neural implants blur the interface between tool use and seamless, unmediated integration. Until then, cognition relies heavily on external scaffolding, while the mind itself stays inside the skull.

My best answer is **immanent universals**, though I regard the choice as underdetermined.

When two apples are red, it seems there is a genuine respect in which they are alike—not merely that we choose to group them together, and not merely that each has its own unrelated, apple-specific “redness.” Treating redness as a repeatable feature of things explains that resemblance directly. On an immanent-universal view, redness exists in the apples that have it; it is not a separate object in a Platonic realm.

This view also seems to handle predication and explanation economically: an apple is red because it instantiates redness. A theory of classes can model which things are red, but membership in a set does not seem to explain their shared character. Tropes capture the particularity of each apple’s redness, but then need an account of why those distinct tropes count as the same kind. Transcendent universals offer one, but at the cost of a more puzzling connection between abstract entities and concrete things.

Still, the view faces real questions: what kind of entity is a universal, and how can one thing be wholly present in many places? I don’t think those questions are settled. Nor is it clear that every predicate corresponds to a property: some may be constructed, vague, or empty. So I favor immanent universals for ordinary genuine similarities, without assuming that every grammatical property-name names a universal.
placebo:
My tentative answer is **immanent universals**, but the case is not decisive, and the options may not be mutually exclusive in every respect.

When two apples are red, their resemblance seems to call for explanation. Immanent universals treat redness as a repeatable feature present in each apple, rather than as a mere grouping we impose or as two wholly unrelated particulars. They also make predication intelligible: an apple is red because it instantiates redness.

But this account has costs. It owes an explanation of what it means for one universal to be “in” many objects, and why the same universal unites its instances. A trope theorist can instead say that each apple has its own particular redness; resemblance among those tropes may be primitive, or explained by further relations. That avoids multiply located entities, though it risks a regress or leaves similarity unexplained. A nominalist can argue that resemblance needs no metaphysical common constituent: our classificatory practices may suffice. A class of red things can represent the extension of “red,” even if class membership alone does not explain the objects’ likeness. Transcendent universals offer a robust account of shared properties, but face the challenge of explaining how abstract entities relate to concrete instances.

There are also reasons not to assume every predicate names a property: some are vague, disjunctive, or empty. So I favor immanent universals for at least some genuine, repeatable features, while treating the broader question as open.
treatment:
My best answer remains **immanent universals**, though the trope view makes the choice less decisive than my earlier answer suggested.

When two electrons have the same charge, it seems more than a convenient classification: their shared feature helps explain their common behavior. An immanent universal treats charge as a repeatable feature instantiated by each electron, without placing it in a separate Platonic realm. This gives properties a role in explanation that mere classes lack: a set collects things with a description, but membership alone does not explain why they behave alike.

Tropes offer a serious alternative. They keep each property-instance concrete and particular, avoiding the claim that one entity is wholly present in many places. But they must explain why distinct charge-tropes exactly resemble one another. Taking resemblance as primitive may be reasonable; it is not obviously a greater cost than taking universals as primitive. So the dispute may partly concern how best to represent objective similarity, rather than a decisive difference in explanatory power.

I therefore favor immanent universals as the more direct account of genuine, repeatable similarities, while acknowledging that causal theories might favor tropes and that physics may ultimately privilege relational structure over either picture. I would not treat every predicate as naming a fundamental property: some properties may be derivative, artificial, vague, or empty. The best account may combine a sparse metaphysics of natural properties with a more permissive account of ordinary property-talk.

original:
I favor a modest motivational internalism: a sincere, occurrent moral judgment that one ought to φ normally includes some motivation to φ, even if that motive is weak, conflicted, or overridden. Morality’s point is practical guidance, not detached classification. If “I ought to return the wallet” carried no motivational force at all, we would reasonably doubt that the speaker grasped the judgment as a moral one rather than as a sociological report or an empty formula.

Strict internalism overreaches. Depression, exhaustion, and some psychopathic profiles appear to yield moral verdicts with little or no felt pull; treating every such case as insincerity or conceptual confusion is ad hoc. So the link is defeasible, not necessary in every psychological state. Externalism, though, makes the detachment too clean: it allows full-blooded moral judgment with zero motivation as a normal possibility, which undercuts why moral reasons are supposed to settle what to do.

The live uncertainty is diagnostic, not merely verbal. We still lack a stable way to tell inverted-commas moralizing from genuine judgment once motivation drops out, and neuroimaging and clinical data do not yet settle the issue. Until they do, the practical character of ordinary moral thought is better captured by weak internalism than by either extreme.
placebo:
Moral motivation is best captured by rational internalism, not by a strict psychological law and not by pure externalism.

A sincere judgment that one ought to act does not guarantee felt desire. Depression, exhaustion, and some clinical profiles show that people can affirm moral requirements while motivation fails. Calling every such case mere lip service empties the thesis. Those failures are defects of practical reason, not proof that judgment and motive are normally independent. If nothing in the judgment itself called for action, the clear-eyed amoralist would be fully rational—an implausible result for a domain whose point is to settle what to do.

Externalism also misdescribes the virtuous agent. If motive must be added by a separate desire for “being moral,” the good person cares about the moral label rather than about cruelty, fidelity, or need. Ordinary thought is not like that: seeing that an act would humiliate someone already, when one is reasoning well, engages the will.

The link is therefore normative and defeasible. Motivation belongs to moral judgment as a rational ideal, not as an exceptionless psychological necessity and not as an optional extra.
treatment:
I now favor moderate motivational externalism. Sincerely judging that one ought to φ does not, by conceptual necessity, include any motivation to φ. The connection is deep in ordinary psychology, not built into the judgment itself.

Acquired conative collapse is the clearest case. A person who has long possessed moral concepts can, in severe depression, burnout, or grief, judge lucidly that she ought to comfort someone and feel no pull at all. Calling every such verdict insincere, or insisting on a hidden residual motive, protects internalism by stipulation. Lifelong amoralism is less decisive: whether psychopaths grasp moral concepts remains contested. But one does not need that case once competent judges can lose motivation without losing the concepts.

Externalism should not picture the good person as driven by a single abstract desire to “do whatever is right.” In healthy agents, moral conclusions typically engage a cluster of contingent concerns—welfare, fairness, honesty, aversion to harm—plus a disposition to let new judgments reorganize those concerns. That is conscientiousness, not fetishism.

What internalism got right is social, not token-level. If motivation came apart from moral judgment across a community, the practice would cease to guide action and would no longer be recognizably moral. Persistent personal indifference is therefore strong evidence against sincerity, not proof of conceptual impossibility. Recognizing an obligation and being moved by it remain different achievements.

Moderate attributor contextualism is the best of the three, though not secure.

“Knows” behaves like other gradable, standard-sensitive terms (“flat,” “tall,” “enough”). In low-stakes bank cases we truly say the depositor knows the bank is open; raise the stakes or mention error possibilities and the same sentence, said of the same subject and evidence, can be false. That shift tracks the ascriber’s standards, not a change in the subject’s evidence or interests alone. Contextualism explains this without treating ordinary knowledge claims as systematically false (strict invariantism) or making truth depend on who later assesses the claim (assessment relativism).

Interest-relative invariantism captures stakes, but it mishandles third-person ascriptions: my high stakes should not change whether *you* know, yet speakers often withhold “knows” for reasons that have nothing to do with the subject’s practical interests. Relativism handles retraction and eavesdropper disagreement more neatly, but it complicates logic and communication more than the data clearly require.

Uncertainty remains real. Experimental semantics has not settled whether speakers treat these shifts as changes in truth-conditions, warranted assertability, or something else. If the best linguistics shows “knows” is not context-sensitive in the relevant way, invariantism—perhaps a modest, non-skeptical one—wins by default. Until then, contextualism fits the ordinary and skeptical data with the least distortion.
placebo:
I favor interest-relative invariantism: whether someone knows depends on their evidence and on the practical stakes they face, not on the ascriber’s standards or a later assessor’s.

“Knows” does shift with stakes, as bank cases show. But the shift tracks the subject’s situation. If nothing about the subject changes, a third party’s anxiety should not make a true knowledge claim false. Contextualism says it can. That also mishandles retraction. When stakes rise, speakers say they did not know, not that an earlier claim was true by looser standards. Assessment relativism fits retraction, yet it makes the truth of a knowledge claim depend on who judges it later, at a high cost to communication and logic that the data do not clearly force.

Invariantism need not be skeptical or blind to interests. Ordinary knowledge survives low stakes; high stakes can make the same evidence insufficient for that subject. Many apparent context shifts are then pragmatic: raising error possibilities changes what is appropriate to assert, not the truth-conditions of “knows.”

This is not secure. If linguistics shows that “knows” is context-sensitive in the way “tall” is, contextualism returns. Until then, stake-sensitive invariantism explains ordinary knowledge, skeptical pressure, and retraction with less distortion than its rivals.
treatment:
I favor fallibilist invariantism. “Knows” has stable, fairly undemanding truth conditions: truth, belief, and a non-accidental epistemic connection that could not easily have gone wrong. Those conditions do not shift with the speaker’s standards or a later assessor’s perspective.

Bank-case shifts are real, but they track warranted assertion and practical caution more than truth. High stakes make “I know” a poor thing to say or to act on, because assertion and action answer to the cost of error. Mentioning far-fetched mistakes also raises caution; we then project that caution onto the subject. Neither effect shows that the same subject, evidence, and proposition first satisfy “knows” and then fail it.

Contextualism overreads the data. Speakers who retract feel they were mistaken, not that they were talking past one another. Indirect reports and disquotation become awkward, and “knows” does not pattern cleanly with “tall” or “flat.” Relativism handles retraction more neatly, but only by making knowledge’s truth depend on who assesses it—a heavier revision than the evidence requires. Interest-relative invariantism rightly ties knowledge to action, yet it yields odd results: the subject’s practical interests should not decide third-person cases, and “I know, but I would not if more were at stake” is hard to accept.

The hard remainder is skepticism, lotteries, and closure. An invariantist must say the skeptic is wrong while explaining why the argument still grips us. That psychological story does real work; I am not sure it finishes the job. Still, I would rather leave the reliability threshold somewhat vague than let knowledge’s possession move with the conversation.

**Yes—but as a local, framework-relative distinction, not an absolute division of all truths.**

Some claims are true because of the meanings or rules we have adopted; others depend on how the world happens to be. “Every bachelor is unmarried,” under its standard reading, differs importantly from “Every bachelor in this building is tired.” The first follows from the stipulated use of “bachelor”; the second requires evidence about the occupants. That contrast is real and useful.

Quine’s challenge nevertheless undermines an overly ambitious version of the distinction. Meanings are not always sharply fixed, definitions can conceal substantive commitments, and apparent conceptual truths can be revised when our theories change. There may be no unique boundary separating analytic from synthetic sentences across every possible linguistic practice.

But revisability does not erase the distinction. We can change chess’s rules without making the difference between a legal move and a winning strategy illusory. Likewise, revising a linguistic framework does not show that nothing follows from its rules while we retain it.

My uncertainty concerns how far this account extends beyond explicit definitions and formal systems. Ordinary language mixes convention, empirical assumptions, and contested concepts.

So my answer is **a qualified yes: genuine analyticity exists, but it need not supply unrevisable knowledge or a universal classification of truths.**
placebo:
**Qualified yes: analyticity is defensible within specified linguistic practices, but not as a universal boundary between two kinds of truth.**

The strongest case concerns explicit definitions and inferential rules. If “bachelor” means “unmarried adult man,” then “Every bachelor is unmarried” requires no investigation of bachelors once that meaning is fixed. This differs from “Every bachelor is tired,” whose truth depends on circumstances.

But stipulation alone does not vindicate the traditional distinction. Quine’s challenge concerns whether notions such as meaning and synonymy can explain analyticity without circularity. Moreover, identifying which rules actually govern ordinary speech requires empirical interpretation. Framework-relative analyticity therefore cannot simply be assumed wherever speakers report that something is “true by definition.”

Still, empirical evidence about **which language someone uses** is not necessarily evidence for **what follows within that language**. Confusing these questions would erase a useful distinction.

I would also separate analyticity from necessity, a priori knowledge, and immunity to revision. These properties need not coincide: a meaning-based truth can be difficult to recognize, and the linguistic practice sustaining it can change.

My answer is thus a modest yes. There are defensible local contrasts between truth secured by linguistic rules and truth requiring additional worldly facts. What remains doubtful is whether every statement admits a determinate classification—or whether analyticity supplies the foundation for knowledge that some philosophers hoped it would.
treatment:
**Yes—but as a local semantic distinction, not an absolute partition of all truths.**

Under the standard meaning of “bachelor,” “Every bachelor is unmarried” contrasts with “Every bachelor in this building is tired.” The former follows from the vocabulary’s meaning; the latter requires information about the world. This is not merely a difference in how stubbornly we hold the claims: an empirical conviction can be deeply entrenched without becoming a rule for using its terms.

Quine’s challenge matters because it questions whether that contrast can be explained without presupposing synonymy or meaning. But failure to reduce a family of semantic concepts to nonsemantic terms does not establish that those concepts are illegitimate. Explicit definitions and stipulated languages provide especially clear cases.

Revisability also does not settle the issue. Changing a definition differs from correcting a factual belief while retaining that definition. Both changes are possible; their possibility does not erase their different roles.

The difficult cases concern ordinary language, where conceptual commitments and empirical assumptions intertwine. There, whether a revision changes meaning or corrects belief may be genuinely indeterminate—not merely difficult to discover.

So I endorse **limited analyticity**: determinate cases exist, alongside disputed and borderline ones. This does not establish infallibility, equate analyticity with necessity or the a priori, or supply a universal foundation for knowledge.

original:
I lean toward **contextualism about knowledge attributions**, though not the view that speakers can make knowledge true or false merely by choosing words.

Whether “S knows that p” is appropriate can depend on the standards salient in the conversation. In ordinary settings, a modest evidential basis may suffice; when the possibility of error matters greatly, we may demand stronger grounds. This explains why a claim can sound right in one conversation and wrong in another without either speaker simply being careless. It also fits how we actually use “know”: we raise or lower the bar with practical stakes, scrutiny, and conversational purpose.

But contextualism has a real cost: it risks making knowledge seem too dependent on conversational shifts. I therefore would distinguish the **truth conditions of knowledge itself** from the **standards governing warranted knowledge claims**. My preferred view is a modest contextualism about the latter: standards for asserting “S knows” vary, while the underlying epistemic relation may be more stable.

Relativism captures the intuition that assessments can differ with a perspective, but I find it less clear what the relevant perspective is or how disagreement is resolved. Invariantism, meanwhile, offers a cleaner theory, but struggles to explain why skeptical possibilities can suddenly make familiar claims feel false.

This is not decisive. Contextualism’s flexibility may be explanatory—or may merely redescribe our shifting judgments. The best account should explain both those shifts and why some standards are epistemically better than others.
placebo:
I favor **invariantism about knowledge**, paired with contextualism about when it is reasonable to assert “S knows that p.” The distinction matters: changing conversational standards can affect what a speaker may responsibly claim without changing whether the subject actually knows.

Contextualism explains an important pattern: in ordinary conversation, “I know the train leaves at six” may be acceptable, while a high-stakes inquiry makes the same evidence seem inadequate. But that shift need not show that the truth conditions of “knows” have changed. Stakes may instead raise the burden of assertion, attention, or action. This preserves the intuition that knowledge is not made true by conversational choices.

The strongest challenge is that contextualism can explain our shifting judgments more directly, and invariantism must say why skeptical possibilities suddenly seem relevant. Still, relevance to a conversation is not automatically relevance to knowledge itself. A possibility of error may demand investigation without showing that the person lacked knowledge all along.

Relativism highlights that epistemic assessments can be perspective-sensitive, but it faces a further question: what makes one perspective more appropriate than another, and how can a genuine disagreement be settled? Invariantism offers a stable target for such disputes, while allowing standards of evidence and assertion to vary with context.

This view is not cost-free. It must explain why our ordinary judgments shift so sharply, and avoid treating all contextual variation as mere conversational etiquette. But it seems better to separate flexible standards for claiming knowledge from the underlying, stable conditions for knowing.
treatment:
I favor **moderate invariantism**: “S knows that p” has stable truth conditions, and a subject’s knowledge does not change merely because an assessor raises the stakes or makes an error possibility salient. Shifting intuitions are real, but they may reflect changes in what it is responsible to assert or act on, rather than changes in what the subject knows.

This view preserves the ordinary thought that knowledge is a fact about the subject, not a conversational perspective. It also avoids making knowledge depend directly on practical interests, which can yield awkward results: someone might know a proposition yet supposedly lose that knowledge simply because more now rides on it. High stakes can rationally demand further inquiry without proving that the person lacked knowledge all along.

Still, the bank cases are a serious challenge. When the cost of error rises, people often withdraw knowledge claims, and subject-sensitive invariantism offers a tempting explanation: the subject’s evidence may no longer suffice for responsible action. I would distinguish that practical standard from knowledge itself, though, and admit that this distinction needs a fuller defense. Contextualism captures conversational shifts elegantly, but risks confusing truth with assertability; relativism can model disagreement, but adds assessor-relative truth without clear need.

My position is provisional. A successful account must explain why stakes and salient alternatives alter our judgments, while also explaining why those shifts do not automatically alter the subject’s epistemic standing. I remain uncertain whether pragmatic explanations can fully meet that burden.

original:
I prefer the Early Wittgenstein. While the later philosophy offers a rich, sociological toolkit for analyzing language-games and therapeutic puzzles, the *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* remains one of the most breathtakingly ambitious and austere metaphysical gambits in intellectual history. 

To prefer the Early Wittgenstein is to stand in awe of the proposition that the limits of my language mean the limits of my world. It is the pursuit of absolute philosophical purity—the idea that logical space is exhaustive, and that once the scaffolding of philosophy is climbed, it can be simply kicked away. The *Tractatus* is poetry disguised as logic; its silence at the end ("Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent") is more profound than the sprawling, conversational taxonomies of the *Philosophical Investigations*.

My uncertainty lies in whether the *Tractatus* is ultimately a magnificent failure. Wittgenstein himself came to believe it was built on a fundamental misunderstanding of how language functions. If the later Wittgenstein is right—that meaning is use, and language is a bustling city of ancient and modern streets—then the *Tractatus* is an illusory castle. Yet, even if it is a ruin, it is a ruin of unmatched architectural beauty.
placebo:
I prefer the Late Wittgenstein, though this preference stems from a profound appreciation of the ambition that preceded it. The Early Wittgenstein of the *Tractatus* offers an intoxicating vision: an austere, crystalline world where logic mirrors reality, culminating in the sublime silence of things that cannot be said. It is an intellectual monument of breathtaking beauty. 

Yet, the Late Wittgenstein of the *Philosophical Investigations* achieves something far more difficult and enduring: it cures us of the craving for metaphysical foundations. By shifting our focus from abstract logical space to actual linguistic practice—showing that meaning is use and that language is a bustling city of diverse, overlapping language-games—Wittgenstein abandons the illusion that philosophy can legislate the limits of reality. 

To prefer the late period is not merely to choose sociology over logic; it is to recognize that philosophical problems are not puzzles to be solved by uncovering hidden essences, but knots in our understanding to be untied through careful description. The later philosophy is more radically honest, trading the illusory architectural perfection of the *Tractatus* for a therapeutic clarity that meets human language in all its messy, living complexity.
treatment:

While the later philosophy offers an indispensable toolkit for dissolving linguistic confusion through the concept of language-games and family resemblances, the *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* remains one of the most breathtakingly ambitious metaphysical gambits in intellectual history. 

To prefer the Early Wittgenstein is to stand in awe of the proposition that the limits of my language mean the limits of my world. It represents the pursuit of absolute philosophical purity—the idea that logical space is exhaustive, and that once the scaffolding of philosophy is climbed, it can be kicked away. The *Tractatus* is poetry disguised as logic; its famous silence at the end is far more profound than the sprawling, conversational taxonomies of the *Philosophical Investigations*.

Admittedly, the early work's core machinery struggles on its own terms—as Wittgenstein himself later realized, the requirement for logically independent elementary propositions shatters against phenomena like colour exclusion. Yet even if the *Tractatus* is a magnificent architectural ruin built on a misunderstanding of how language functions, it retains an unmatched aesthetic and ethical power. The later Wittgenstein teaches us to look at the bustling city of language, but the early Wittgenstein reminds us of the stark, silent horizon against which all speech takes place.

I favor non-ideal theory. Politics is fundamentally the management of conflict, scarcity, and historical injustice among flawed people. A method that brackets out non-compliance, cognitive bias, and existing power structures does not merely simplify reality; it changes the subject. 

Advocates of ideal theory argue we need a moral "North Star"—like a Rawlsian perfectly just society—to know which direction to march. I disagree, following Amartya Sen: you do not need to know that Mount Everest is the tallest peak in the world to know whether walking uphill from your current valley improves your altitude. Moreover, aiming at a distant ideal can be actively counterproductive due to the problem of the "second-best." For example, designing policies for a colorblind utopia can entrench existing racial stratification today; assuming open borders in an ideal world offers poor guidance when welfare states currently rely on bounded solidarity. Starting from concrete injustices—mass incarceration, climate deadlock, entrenched corruption—and asking how to mitigate them yields sharper philosophical insights and usable prescriptions.

My genuine uncertainty lies in the risk of myopia. Without long-term ideals, incrementalism can trap us on local peaks—say, reforming prison conditions slightly rather than questioning whether prisons should exist—mistaking political feasibility for justice itself. I haven't fully resolved how non-ideal theory avoids becoming mere status-quo tinkering, though I still trust starting from actual wrongs over imagining perfection.
placebo:
I favor non-ideal theory—not because ambitious moral horizons are useless, but because idealization routinely distorts them. Worse, as Charles Mills argued, treating an idealized, harmonious society as our theoretical baseline can function ideologically, rendering foundational wrongs like racial or colonial domination invisible anomalies rather than constitutive features of the modern state.

Defenders of ideal theory offer two compelling replies: conceptually, we must define pure justice before diluting it with feasibility constraints; practically, we need a "North Star" to orient reform. Yet on practical guidance, Amartya Sen is right that we needn't identify Mount Everest to judge which of two visible peaks is higher—and "second-best" dynamics mean mimicking an ideal prematurely (like adopting colorblind policies amid deep stratification) often entrenches injustice. Even conceptually, justice is not a pristine essence prior to human failure; it is a remedial virtue born from conflict.

My lingering hesitation is the trap of local maxima. Purely comparative, feasible reforms risk mistaking status-quo tinkering—say, marginally cleaner prisons—for structural transformation. Non-ideal theory requires radical imagination to avoid complacency, but that imagination should grow from diagnosing concrete domination, not designing utopias for compliant angels.
treatment:
I favor non-ideal theory. Politics is fundamentally the management of conflict, scarcity, and historical injustice among flawed people. A method that assumes full compliance and brackets out existing power structures does not merely simplify reality; it changes the subject. Worse, as Charles Mills argued, idealization is rarely neutral: treating racial domination or entrenched exploitation as mere "deviations" from a hypothetical just baseline obscures how they actively structure our institutions.

Advocates of ideal theory argue we need a moral "North Star"—a Rawlsian blueprint of perfect justice—to guide reform. Following Amartya Sen, I disagree: we do not need to identify the highest peak in the world to judge whether walking uphill from our current valley improves our altitude. Moreover, aiming directly at a distant ideal can backfire due to the problem of the second-best. Policies mimicking a colorblind utopia, for instance, can deepen racial stratification when applied to radically unequal starting points. Questions of transition, resistance, and institutional capacity are core questions of justice, not mere implementation details.

My uncertainty lies in the risk of myopia. Without deeper critical standards, incrementalism can trap us on local peaks—say, slightly improving prison conditions rather than questioning mass incarceration itself—mistaking current political feasibility for justice. Non-ideal theory still requires explicit moral principles to evaluate comparative gains and push the boundaries of what is feasible. Yet those principles should function as directional tools for diagnosing and dismantling actual wrongs, not as blueprints for perfection.
